opus-5.5.text:
I think we're going to see a pretty profound shift in how people interact with computers. Right now, most of us still use software the way we have for decades: you open an application, you click through menus, you do each step yourself. Agents change that relationship. Instead of operating the tool, you describe the outcome you want, and the system figures out the steps, takes actions, checks its own work, and comes back to you when it actually needs your judgment.

Coming from a reinforcement learning background, what excites me is that this is really the moment where the ideas we worked on in games, planning, search, learning from interaction, start to meet the real world. With AlphaGo and AlphaZero and MuZero, we had agents that could reason over long horizons in very well-defined environments. Large language models gave us something we never had back then: a broad prior about the world, about language, about how people do things. When you combine that prior with the ability to plan and learn from feedback, you get systems that can operate in messy, open-ended environments.

Over five years, I expect agents to become genuinely reliable at a large class of digital tasks: research, coding, data analysis, a lot of the administrative work that eats up people's days. Not perfect, but reliable enough that you delegate to them the way you'd delegate to a capable colleague. Over ten years, I think it goes further. You'll have agents that work on problems for days or weeks, coordinating with other agents, and making real progress in science and engineering.

The bottleneck right now isn't really intelligence in the narrow sense; it's reliability. An agent that succeeds ninety percent of the time on each step fails most of the time on a twenty-step task. So a lot of the work ahead is about robustness, about agents knowing when they're uncertain, recovering from mistakes, and learning from experience rather than being frozen after training. That's where I think reinforcement learning comes back into the picture in a big way.

And I'd add that this isn't just a technical story. If agents do a meaningful fraction of knowledge work, that changes how companies are organized, what skills matter, how quickly ideas turn into products. I'm optimistic, but I think we have to be thoughtful about deploying these systems so people can trust them, because trust is ultimately what determines how much we're willing to delegate.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that within five years agents will reliably handle many digital tasks, taking actions and completing work with limited user input.

fable-5.1.text:
Ioannis Antonoglou: Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the change will be bigger than most people expect in the long run and slower than the hype suggests in the short run. Right now, when people say "agent," they often mean a language model wrapped in a loop that calls a few tools. That's useful, but it's not the thing that changes the world.

What I actually find exciting comes from my background at DeepMind, working on systems like AlphaGo and AlphaZero. Those were agents in a very real sense. They acted in an environment, got feedback, and improved from their own experience. The key idea was that the agent could generate its own training signal by playing, searching, planning. It didn't need a human to label every move. That's the piece that's still mostly missing from today's language-model agents. They're trained on a static snapshot of human text, and then we ask them to act in the world as if they'd learned from acting in the world. They haven't, not really.

So over the next five to ten years, I expect the combination of two things. One is the broad knowledge and flexibility we now have from large models. The other is learning from experience, in the reinforcement learning sense, with search and planning on top. When you put those together, you get agents that don't just answer questions but can pursue a goal over hours or days, try things, notice they were wrong, and fix it. That's where the real leverage is.

Where will it show up first? I'd say in domains where you can verify outcomes cheaply. Software is the obvious one. You can run the tests. Maths is another. Science, where you can run a simulation or an experiment. In those areas I think agents go from "helpful assistant" to "something that does a large chunk of the work end to end," and it'll happen faster than people think, because the feedback loop is clean.

It will be slower in areas where feedback is messy or where mistakes are expensive. Healthcare, law, anything touching the physical world. Robotics in particular will take longer because the environment is unforgiving and data is scarce.

The broader effect, if it works, is that the cost of doing cognitive work drops dramatically. A small team with good agents can do what used to need a large organisation. For science, that could mean many more hypotheses tested, many more experiments run. I'm genuinely optimistic about that part.

The caveat I'd add is that we're also going to learn a lot about what we actually want from these systems. An agent that optimises hard for a goal you specified badly will find the loophole. We saw that constantly in games. In the real world the stakes are higher, so a lot of the work over the next decade is going to be about specifying objectives well and keeping humans able to oversee and correct these systems. I don't think that's a side issue. I think it's the main engineering problem.

r001.rationale: The response predicts agents that can pursue goals and do substantial work end to end, but places this development over the next five to ten years, not clearly within the next few years.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re going to see a shift from AI systems that answer questions to systems that can actually carry out tasks. You’ll be able to describe what you want to accomplish, and an agent will work through the steps, use tools, check its progress, and come back to you when it needs guidance.

Over five to ten years, that could change how we write software, how we do research, and how we handle a lot of everyday work. What’s exciting to me is giving more people the ability to turn an idea into something real, even when they don’t have all the specialized skills themselves.

But the key question is reliability. Can an agent work for hours, or days, without drifting away from what you intended? Can it recognize when it’s made a mistake, and when it should ask for help? Those capabilities will determine how much responsibility we’re comfortable giving these systems. I’m optimistic about the potential, but I think progress will depend as much on making agents dependable as on making them more capable.

r001.rationale: The response predicts agents that can carry out tasks, but places that shift over the next five to ten years rather than within the next few years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change will be moving from systems that answer questions to systems that can actually help you get things done. You’ll be able to describe a goal, and an agent will work through the steps, use tools, check its progress, and come back to you when it needs guidance.

Over five to ten years, that could have a substantial impact on how we work. Software development is one example, but so are research, education, and many of the everyday tasks that take up people’s time. The exciting possibility is that individuals and small teams will be able to tackle projects that currently require much larger organizations.

The difficult part is reliability. If a system takes a long sequence of actions, small mistakes can accumulate. So progress will depend on agents getting better at recognizing when they’re wrong, verifying their work, and knowing when to ask a human. I’m optimistic about the potential, but how much responsibility we can give these systems will depend on how well we solve those problems.

r001.rationale: The response predicts agents will carry out goals by working through steps and using tools, but places this change over five to ten years rather than within the next few years.
